events.text:
🇾🇪🆒🚫🇸🇦🛢⚡️ ALSAA ANALYSYS ​ The Houthis have just put Saudi Arabia under severe pressure regarding oil.
Seven weeks. That is how long it took Yemeni forces to bring Saudi production down to its lowest level since 1990.
​The timeline:
• July 25 — First direct strikes on Saudi territory since 2022. Jizan and Yanbu hit on the same day. The Jizan refinery (400,000 bpd) brought to a standstill.
• July 27 — Abqaiq on fire. The largest crude stabilization plant in the world.
• August — Jizan remains unserviceable, repeatedly struck.
• September 8 — Massive wave on Abha, Najran, Jizan. 73 injured.
• September 10 — The most strategic blow: the East-West pipeline pumping stations (7 mbpd) hit. The only real alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which is already severely disrupted on the Iranian side. Precautionary shutdown.
​The result:
Hormuz severely disrupted + Red Sea under permanent threat = Saudi Arabia's two main export routes are simultaneously under constraint.
Production: 6.24 mbpd in August → -1.9 mbpd. 
Lowest level in 35 years.
Exports: dropped to 3.2–3.5 mbpd.
Even bypassing comes at a high cost: insurers are pushing premiums up to 3% of the vessel's value on Saudi routes (compared to 0.3% previously), adding +$7–8 per barrel. Many are now rerouting via the Cape of Good Hope → +2 to 4 weeks of transit time.
​The bill:
≈ $200 million/day in lost revenue from lost production.
Jizan alone: ≈ $42 million/day.
For the month of August alone: around $6 billion in potential revenues lost.
​Two strategic corridors put under pressure at the same time.
​The Houthis hit where it hurts most.

🪖🇬🇧Britain sanctions Israeli settlers — while keeping Israel’s military machine close
 
Days before London announced sanctions on Israeli settlers, more than 300 British soldiers took part in Pegasus Athena, a major training exercise facilitated by Elbit Systems UK, the British subsidiary of Israeli defense giant Elbit Systems.
👉 That is just one example of how deeply Israel’s defense industry is embedded in Britain’s military — raising serious questions about whether London can claim to oppose the occupation while maintaining such extensive military ties with Israel.
 
Elbit’s involvement goes far beyond Pegasus Athena:
🟥 $138m — a five-year MoD contract awarded in 2021 for a system allowing frontline troops to detect and engage targets within seconds.
🟥 $139m — a 2021 contract for the Maritime Electronic Warfare System, providing anti-missile defense for British warships, including Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carriers and Type 45 destroyers.
🟥 $88m — a 12-year contract awarded in 2021 to an Elbit-linked joint venture to operate training aircraft for Britain’s Military Flying Training System.
🟥 $19m — a 2023 contract for ground-based surveillance radar systems delivered to the Royal Artillery.
🟥 $16m — an initial contract for night-vision equipment supplied to the British Army by Elbit subsidiary Instro Precision, followed by more than $22m in additional orders.
🟥 $2.7bn — the value of the Watchkeeper drone program overseen by U-TacS, a joint venture involving Elbit UK.
 
And Elbit is only one part of the picture. Rafael, Israel’s state-owned defense company, has also secured major British contracts:
♦️ $51m — a 2024 MoD contract for counter-drone systems.
♦️ $27m — a 2023 contract for protection systems for Britain’s Challenger 3 tanks.
Rafael supplies key technology for Sky Sabre, Britain’s air-defense system, including systems deployed at sensitive sites such as the Falklands.
Its Litening targeting pods are used by RAF Eurofighter Typhoons.
Its UK subsidiary Pearson Engineering secured a $14m contract for mine-clearing equipment for the British Army.
Then there is Project HEZUK — a secret UK-Israel defense program developed in 2019 to counter Iran and Hezbollah.
The cooperation reportedly covered:
🔴 Autonomous warfare
🔴 Space
🔴 Maritime capabilities
🔴 Quantum technologies and advanced manufacturing
🔴 Potential energy weapons and other advanced defense systems
 
The military relationship is only part of it. Britain’s intelligence ties with Israel are also set to remain intact, with no indication that the 2020 UK-Israel military cooperation agreement or the 2023 bilateral relations roadmap will be suspended.
 
The International Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Israel’s occupation is unlawful and said states must not provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by the occupation. Yet Britain continues to train with, buy from, and develop military capabilities alongside Israel’s defense industry.

🪖Could Ansar Allah’s military gains push Gulf states into a new security pact with Iran?
Ansar Allah (Houthis)' blitzkrieg to Mokha and Yemen's western coast has killed several birds with one stone, siezing control over Bab el-Mandeb, giving a lesson to Saudi Arabia, nixing the UAE-Israeli surveillance bid, and potentially opening the door to a new West Asian security architecture.
Saudi Arabia's major push against the Yemenis, which started with Trump-blessed airstrikes on Sanaa in July, has so far ended up miserably: neither the US nor Pakistan has met Riyadh's request for military backing in [its new round of the Yemen war.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74276)
Meanwhile:
♦️ Ansar Allah has liberated the[ strategic port of Mokha](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74480), the surrounding region, the coastline down to Bab el-Mandeb, and[ a number of key islands in the Red Sea.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74392)
♦️ Attacks on S[audi Arabia's trans-Indo-Pacific East-West oil pipeline](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74389), used by Riyadh to circumvent the nearly completely closed Strait of Hormuz, forced the Saudis to shut it down. The pipeline carried Saudi oil from Abqaiq to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
♦️ Saudi Arabia's extensive network of mercenary forces in [Western Yemen has de facto collapsed.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74329)
Ansar Allah's capture of vital islands in the Red Sea has serious geostrategic consequences:
🌏 The Houthis' capture of the strategically important island of Perim, which sits at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, gives them ultimate control of the waterway.
🌏 The reported liberation of Zuqar – part of the Hanish Islands – appears to have undermined Emirati-Israeli spy efforts in the region, military experts claim.
In October 2025, satellite images showed an [airstrip built on Zuqar](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/58447), a strategic island in the Red Sea about 88.5 km south of the port of Hodeidah, held by the Houthis. AP reported at the time that the UAE was involved in the military construction project, aimed at establishing a launching point against Ansar Allah and surveillance over its activities in the Red Sea and the nearby coastline. The construction reportedly started in April 2025.
‼️ A strategic foothold by the UAE in the Red Sea would have enabled the Israeli-UAE Hexagon Alliance, aka the Abraham Accords Axis, to exert pressure on Yemen, making its liberation crucial for Ansar Allah.
Persian Gulf states meeting in Oman
A September 14 meeting in Muscat bringing together Iran, Iraq, and other countries bordering the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman has been announced by Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei on Friday.
Baghaei noted that Iran had sought to build regional trust and cooperation for peace and stability, free from “destructive and divisive” outside intervention. He also stressed that the meeting would address the outcome of Iran-Oman talks on commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The timing, which coincided with successful Houthi advancements, is telling.
If Saudi Arabia and other regional powers attend the meeting, it will be game over for Trump's ambitions in the Gulf as well as for US and Israeli war planners' dream to keep the region under their military control, geopolitical observers say. At the same time, it could open the door to a new regional security architecture.

📉 🇺🇸 US cuts back its air cover for tankers in Hormuz—report
🔊Since early September, the US has restricted its protection window in the Strait of Hormuz to just two designated time slots per day, the FT reports.
The change was communicated by the US naval coordination center to maritime advisers, with tanker operators encouraged to plan their transits around specific departure times — 9am, for example — if they want to be covered by US aircraft.
Until recently, ships using the route along Oman’s coast could request US protection and receive coordinates for transit during broad overnight windows.
US officials acknowledge that traveling through the strait under cover of darkness has become less secure, while maintaining continuous air protection is costly. A US military aircraft can cost tens of thousands of dollars per hour to operate.
This time shift came about as Iran has stepped up pressure on shipping in response to US and Israeli attacks, with Tehran also announcing plans for a “restricted zone” in the strait.
In Hormuz, US protection has office hours.
